scope_note: Every text-to-speech system that matters in 2026 — hosted APIs, hyperscaler services, open-weights models, on-device engines, realtime speech-to-speech and voice conversion — on the axes that actually decide a project: what it sounds like, what it costs, what hardware it needs, what you are legally allowed to do with it, and where it quietly falls over.
method_note: Compiled from primary sources: vendor pricing and documentation pages, Hugging Face model cards, GitHub repositories, papers and public leaderboards. Azure figures come from the Azure Retail Prices API and AWS figures from the AWS Price List API rather than the pricing pages, which render via JavaScript and show placeholders to scrapers — the reason many published comparisons carry stale Azure numbers. Every pricing, latency and licence claim was re-checked against primary sources by a second pass instructed to refute rather than confirm. Where a figure could not be verified it is marked as such rather than smoothed over.

systems.name: IBM Watson TTS

Expressive voices add speaking styles (GoodNews, Apology, Uncertainty), automatic emphasis of interjections and emphasis of specified words; with expressive voices <prosody> supports percentage values ONLY. systems.name: Meta
systems.cloning: Not a product capability; Voicebox was never released
systems.emotion: Expression transfer through translation, not authored control
systems.runs_on: Self-hosted GPU; Meta operates no TTS API
systems.latency_note: ~2 s for streaming translation, not TTS
systems.best_for: Speech-to-speech translation research, including expression transfer and simultaneous streaming translation.
systems.watch: Meta has shipped nothing in speech since December 2023 — every 2025–26 release from the facebook org is vision, 3D or robotics. CC-BY-NC prohibits commercial use outright; this is a hard block, not a "verify first".

systems.params: SeamlessM4T v2 Large: 2.3 B (Meta's model card)
systems.architecture: SeamlessM4T v2 uses a non-autoregressive text-to-unit decoder for improved text/speech consistency, and is the foundation for SeamlessExpressive (preserves pauses, speech rate, vocal style and emotional tone across translation) and SeamlessStreaming (simultaneous translation)
systems.streaming: SeamlessStreaming supports simultaneous translation streaming; no streaming documented for a TTS path
systems.billing_unit: N/A — free/self-host; Meta operates no commercial TTS API

systems.ssml: None — expression transfer through translation, with no SSML or instruction interface
systems.lexicon: None
systems.benchmarks: Meta reported state-of-the-art translation and transcription results at release (2023); no current 2026 arena, MOS or comparable TTS benchmark position. SeamlessStreaming delivers translations at ~2 s latency (Meta's figure, for translation not TTS, no hardware stated).
systems.released: SeamlessM4T August 2023; SeamlessM4T v2, SeamlessExpressive, SeamlessStreaming and the unified Seamless model December 2023. No new Meta speech or TTS release found in 2026 — enumerating the 60 most recent facebook-org Hugging Face models (2025-12 to 2026-06) on 2026-07-31 returned only vision, 3D, segmentation, depth, keypoint and robotics models.

systems.name: Meta MMS-TTS
systems.cloning: No — one fixed single-speaker checkpoint per language (config.json: num_speakers 1, speaker_embedding_size 0). No reference-audio path exists.
systems.emotion: None — no emotion or style interface. VitsConfig exposes speaking_rate and noise_scale, which change pace and randomness, not affect.
systems.languages_note: 1,107 languages, one independently trained checkpoint each
systems.runs_on: CPU or GPU — 36.3 M-parameter checkpoint; Hugging Face's official VITS example runs it in plain PyTorch with no accelerator specified
systems.best_for: Text-to-speech in long-tail languages nothing else covers. It is frequently the only way to synthesise a given language at all, and each checkpoint is small enough to run without a GPU. Research and other non-commercial use only.
systems.watch: CC-BY-NC 4.0 forbids commercial use — a hard block, not a 'verify first', and the same block that applies to Seamless. Output is 16 kHz (config.json sampling_rate: 16000), well below the 24–48 kHz of current TTS models. Training data is drawn largely from religious texts (arXiv 2305.13516), so register and vocabulary skew accordingly. Per-language quality across the 1,107-language tail is uneven and, for most of that tail, unbenchmarked.
systems.standout: 1,107 languages as real TTS checkpoints at 36 M parameters each — for most of that tail, the only way to synthesise the language at all
systems.params: 36,284,592 (facebook/mms-tts-eng); 36,282,096 (facebook/mms-tts-kor). One separate checkpoint per language, not a single multilingual model — a 1,107-language deployment means 1,107 checkpoints.
systems.architecture: VITS — end-to-end variational inference with adversarial learning and normalizing flows, hidden_size 192, HiFi-GAN decoder, stochastic duration prediction. Trained per language.
systems.streaming: None documented — VitsModel returns a complete waveform tensor.
systems.billing_unit: N/A — free / self-host; Meta operates no TTS API
systems.self_host: Yes — weights on Hugging Face as facebook/mms-tts-<iso3> and in the facebook/mms-tts umbrella repo; supported in transformers via VitsModel. No Meta API, no SLA, no support.
systems.ssml: None
systems.lexicon: None — no pronunciation override. Non-Roman scripts are romanised with the external uroman package before tokenisation.
systems.released: Announced 22 May 2023 (Meta AI blog; arXiv 2305.13516). facebook/mms-tts Hugging Face repo created 4 June 2023, last modified 25 July 2023 — unchanged since.

systems.name: VoxCPM2
systems.cloning: Zero-shot, reference+transcript mode, AND voice design from text with no reference at all
systems.emotion: Natural-language voice design plus style steering
systems.languages_note: 30 plus Chinese dialects, with automatic detection
systems.runs_on: GPU, ~8 GB VRAM
systems.latency_note: RTF 0.30 on an RTX 4090; 0.13 with Nano-vLLM
systems.best_for: The strongest genuinely commercial-usable open model of 2026 — native 48 kHz with no external upsampler, 1.0 M downloads a month.
systems.watch: The 8 GB VRAM floor rules out CPU and most edge deployment, and no ONNX or GGUF export is documented.
systems.standout: Tokenizer-free and codec-free, native 48 kHz with no external upsampler
systems.params: 2 B (MiniCPM-4 backbone)
systems.architecture: Tokenizer-free diffusion-autoregressive — LocEnc → TSLM → RALM → LocDiT, with AudioVAE V2 and built-in super-resolution; native 48 kHz with no external upsampler
systems.codec: None — tokenizer-free/codec-free; generates continuous speech representations via AudioVAE V2
systems.vram: ~8 GB (Python 3.10-3.12, PyTorch >=2.5, CUDA >=12.0)
systems.streaming: Yes — real-time streaming documented; granularity not stated
systems.quantisation: None documented — no ONNX or GGUF export
systems.watermark: None disclosed (the survey states only the Chatterbox and NeuTTS families ship built-in watermarking)
systems.self_host: Genuine self-hosted deployment; Apache-2.0 weights
systems.lexicon: No phonemizer — takes raw text with automatic language detection and no language tags (which also sidesteps the transitive eSpeak GPL question)
systems.benchmarks: Seed-TTS-eval: 1.84% English WER; 8.13% CER on the hard test set; 1.68% average error across a 30-language multilingual ASR benchmark. RTF ~0.30 on an RTX 4090, ~0.13 with Nano-vLLM on the same card.
systems.adoption: ~1.0 M HF downloads/mo; 34.7k GitHub stars; trained on 2M+ hours
systems.released: 2026-04-06 (multiple secondary sources agree)

systems.name: VoxCPM-0.5B
systems.cloning: Zero-shot from a short reference clip, carrying accent, emotional tone, rhythm and pacing. Continuation-only per the vendor's own comparison table — the isolated-reference mode arrived in VoxCPM2. No minimum reference length is published anywhere.
systems.emotion: No explicit control. Prosody is inferred from the text; emotional tone only carries across from the cloning reference. The vendor lists this as a known limitation.
systems.languages_note: Two — Chinese and English, from a 1.8 M-hour bilingual corpus. The 30-language coverage belongs to VoxCPM2; do not read it back onto this checkpoint.
systems.runs_on: CUDA GPU, ~5 GB VRAM. Not the CPU-friendly sibling of VoxCPM2 that its size implies.
systems.latency_note: RTF "as low as" 0.17 streaming on an RTX 4090 (vendor); ~0.10 under Nano-vLLM
systems.best_for: Reproducing or citing arXiv:2509.24650 (ICLR 2026), which evaluates this checkpoint specifically, and small bilingual zh/en cloning where cleanly Apache-2.0 weights matter more than output bandwidth. For anything new, start at VoxCPM2 instead.
systems.watch: Officially Legacy — the vendor's own table says so, and it has been superseded twice (VoxCPM1.5 Dec 2025, VoxCPM2 Apr 2026). You will learn none of that from the Hugging Face page you land on: main has not moved since 2025-09-19 and the community PR adding the pointer has sat open for two months. Hard ceiling of 16 kHz output against VoxCPM2's 48 kHz. Licence and vendor advice also diverge — the GitHub README markets it as free for commercial use while the model card's Risks section calls it a research release.
systems.standout: The exact checkpoint the VoxCPM paper evaluates — the one to cite or reproduce.
systems.params: 0.5 B backbone (MiniCPM4-0.5B) — that is the vendor's "Backbone Parameters" column, not the whole system, which is ~0.8 B once the 1.30 GB checkpoint and 301 MB AudioVAE are counted
systems.architecture: Tokenizer-free diffusion-autoregressive on a MiniCPM-4 0.5B backbone — LocEnc → TSLM → RALM → LocDiT, trained end-to-end under one diffusion objective with gradients passed through an FSQ bottleneck by straight-through estimation. No external speech tokenizer.
systems.codec: None — tokenizer-free; 16 kHz output via AudioVAE
systems.vram: ~5 GB
systems.streaming: Yes — vendor quotes RTF "as low as" 0.17 on an RTX 4090
systems.quantisation: No official quants. Third-party GGUF (bluryar/VoxCPM-GGUF, Apache-2.0) gives a CPU path — Q4_K 500 MB, Q8_0 803 MB, F16 1.46 GB, plus -audiovae-f16 builds needed for the full pipeline.
systems.fine_tuning: Vendor table marks SFT / LoRA supported. No first-party recipe is linked for this checkpoint, and the HF discussion asking how has been open unanswered for ~11 months.
systems.self_host: Self-host is the only option — pip install voxcpm, or the third-party VoxCPM.cpp GGUF build
systems.benchmarks: Vendor-reported. Seed-TTS-eval: 0.93% CER / 77.2 SIM (zh), 1.85% WER / 72.9 SIM (en), 8.87% CER / 73.0 SIM (hard) — the hard set is the one row the card shows it losing, to CosyVoice2 at 6.83%. CV3-eval: 3.40% CER (zh), 4.04% WER (en).
systems.adoption: 808 likes, 3,090 downloads in the trailing month (checked 2026-08-01) — still real traffic ten months after release and four months after VoxCPM2 replaced it
systems.released: 2025-09-16 (HF repo created); paper arXiv:2509.24650 submitted 2025-09-29

systems.name: Qwen3-TTS
systems.cloning: Zero-shot from 3 seconds
systems.emotion: Natural-language voice design, plus instruction control over 9 preset timbres
systems.runs_on: GPU; the 0.6 B variant is the small-footprint option
systems.latency_note: 97 ms claimed, with no hardware stated
systems.best_for: Commercial realtime voice agents at the 1–2 B scale — Apache-2.0, 3-second cloning and streaming from a single model.
systems.watch: Alibaba has since pivoted its flagship audio models to a closed API, so long-term open support is uncertain.
systems.standout: Apache-2.0 3-second cloning, voice design and streaming from one 0.6-1.7 B model
systems.params: 1.7 B and 0.6 B variants (HF lists the 1.7 B repo at ~2 B tensor size); the tokenizer repo is ~300 M
systems.architecture: Discrete multi-codebook LM, lightweight non-DiT, dual-track hybrid streaming generation — Talker (28 layers, first codebook token from text) + Code Predictor (5 layers, 15 further codebook tokens). Post-training DPO → GSPO. Trained on 5M+ hours.
systems.codec: Qwen3-TTS-Tokenizer-12Hz — 12.5 Hz multi-codebook, jointly optimised semantic + acoustic streams, GAN framework with a WavLM teacher, causal chunked decode, 24 kHz output
systems.vram: Not published by Alibaba. Corpus deployment notes give ~4 GB FP16 for the 0.6 B (6-8 GB with the tokenizer loaded) and ~4.5-6 GB for the 1.7 B (8-10 GB with tokenizer); ~8 GB / ~12 GB for LoRA training.
systems.streaming: Yes — streaming and non-streaming from a single model (dual-track hybrid streaming generation)
systems.max_generation: 10 min continuous per the corpus deployment matrix; not restated on the primary model card
systems.quantisation: Listed among the TTS families carried as GGUF in the audio.cpp-gguf collection; no official quantised build documented by Alibaba
systems.fine_tuning: The Base variants (1.7B-Base / 0.6B-Base) are explicitly designed for fine-tuning — standard HF Trainer, LoRA or full FT, LORA_SCALE at inference; ~5 min of data. Emotion/NL-instruction control weakens after fine-tuning. CustomVoice does not support cloning and Base does not support NL instructions.
systems.self_host: Genuine self-hosted deployment; Apache-2.0 weights across six repos (1.7B VoiceDesign/CustomVoice/Base, 0.6B CustomVoice/Base, tokenizer)
systems.lexicon: Not documented
systems.benchmarks: Seed-TTS-eval: 0.77 WER Chinese, 1.24 WER English. End-to-end synthesis latency as low as 97 ms with no hardware stated. Community fork faster-qwen3-tts (static cache + CUDA graphs): RTF 5.56 and TTFA 152 ms on an RTX 4090; RTF 4.19 on an H100; RTF 0.175→1.57 and TTFA 2.6 s→556 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin.
systems.adoption: ~2.45 M HF downloads/mo on the 1.7B CustomVoice repo alone; 12.7k GitHub stars

systems.name: MOSS-TTS
systems.variants: v1.5 (8 B Delay, Local) and v1.0 (Realtime, Nano)
systems.cloning: Zero-shot; v1.5 targets similarity variance and long-reference/short-text
systems.emotion: Punctuation-driven prosody, inline explicit pause markers (e.g. [pause 3.2s], v1.5 only), token-level duration control, Pinyin and IPA
systems.languages_note: 31 on the v1.5 checkpoints ONLY. The v1.0 checkpoints and MOSS-TTS-Nano are 20 — do not read 31 across the family.
systems.runs_on: 8 B needs a datacentre GPU; the 0.1 B Nano runs realtime on a single CPU core
systems.latency_note: 180 ms TTFB with RTF 0.51 (Realtime variant), no hardware stated
systems.best_for: Covering the whole size range from one family, with native 48 kHz STEREO output — essentially unique among open TTS.
systems.watch: Release-date documentation is inconsistent across the repo, paper and community trackers, and the family naming is confusing.
systems.standout: One Apache-2.0 family from an 8 B datacentre model down to 0.1 B on one CPU core
systems.params: 8 B (MossTTSDelay), 4 B and 1.7 B (MossTTSLocal), 1.7 B (MossTTSRealtime), 0.1 B (MOSS-TTS-Nano). v1.5 exists for only two of these — MOSS-TTS-v1.5 (8 B Delay) and MOSS-TTS-Local-Transformer-v1.5; Realtime and Nano-100M remain at v1.0.
systems.architecture: Three complementary designs — MossTTSDelay (multi-head parallel RVQ prediction with delay-pattern scheduling, for stability/speed), MossTTSLocal (time-synchronous RVQ blocks with a depth transformer, for streaming flexibility), MossTTSRealtime (hierarchical text-audio inputs for low-latency agents)
systems.codec: MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer-v2, native 48 kHz stereo (which v1.5 checkpoints output 48 kHz stereo vs 24 kHz mono is flagged as unresolved in the corpus)
systems.streaming: Yes — streaming output via SGLang-Omni and vLLM-Omni backends; the 0.1 B Nano has built-in streaming
systems.quantisation: ONNX build available for the 0.1 B Nano variant
systems.self_host: Genuine self-hosted deployment; Apache-2.0 across the family (9 model variants including MOSS-TTSD, MOSS-VoiceGenerator, MOSS-SoundEffect)
systems.lexicon: Pinyin and IPA pronunciation control, plus explicit inline [pause X.Ys] markers and token-level duration control
systems.multi_speaker: MOSS-TTSD dialogue model in the family (named in the control-surface table alongside VibeVoice and Dia as the open models with multi-speaker support)
systems.benchmarks: Seed-TTS-eval: English 1.84% WER / 70.86% speaker similarity; Mandarin 1.37% CER / 76.98% similarity. MOSS-TTS-Realtime: 180 ms TTFB with RTF 0.51, ~377 ms total when chained with an LLM — hardware not stated. MOSS-TTSD-v1.0 claims Elo above top proprietary systems in subjective eval (self-reported).
systems.adoption: ~121 k HF downloads/mo on v1.5; 3.9-4.0k GitHub stars on the main repo
systems.released: Technical report arXiv 2603.18090 (March 2026); a community tracker dates the v1.5 weight release to 2026-05-25; MOSS-TTS-Nano 2026-04-10. Exact v1.5 date inconsistent across sources.

systems.name: MOSS-TTS-Realtime
systems.price_note: Free / self-host. A hosted API exists at MOSI AI Studio; its rates are not on the card.
systems.cloning: Reference-audio cloning held consistent across multi-turn dialogue — the card claims strong speaker identity across turns and the config exposes a dedicated reference_audio_pad token. Required reference length is not published.
systems.emotion: No explicit tags or instruction control on this checkpoint. Expressiveness is emergent — it conditions on prior turns' text and acoustics, so prosody adapts to context rather than to a knob. The explicit pause markers belong to MOSS-TTS-v1.5, a different checkpoint.
systems.languages_note: 20 — Chinese, English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Italian, Hebrew, Korean, Russian, Persian, Arabic, Polish, Portuguese, Czech, Danish, Swedish, Hungarian, Greek, Turkish
systems.runs_on: One CUDA GPU. Vendor latency is measured on a single NVIDIA L20 with SDPA + torch.compile; the bf16 checkpoint is 4.66 GB on disk. No official VRAM floor is published.
systems.latency_note: TTFB 180 ms after warm-up, RTF 0.51, on a single NVIDIA L20 with SDPA + torch.compile
systems.best_for: Giving an open LLM voice agent its speech leg — streaming text in, streaming 24 kHz out at ~180 ms TTFB, conditioned on prior turns so voice and prosody stay coherent across a 40-minute conversation. Choose it over batch MOSS-TTS when turn latency and cross-turn consistency matter more than single-shot fidelity.
systems.watch: Named "Realtime" but it is NOT full-duplex speech-to-speech. The words "duplex", "barge" and "interrupt" appear nowhere in any of the four primary documents — there is no listening and no interruption. This is the TTS leg of an agent, not the agent. The headline 377 ms already assumes a separate LLM, and the vendor's own decomposition says so — 197 ms (Qwen3.5-9B on vLLM, first sentence) + 180 ms (TTS). The 180 ms is also explicitly "after warm up".
systems.standout: The only MOSS family member with published latency figures — and they name their hardware.
systems.params: 1.7 B backbone + 200 M local "Depth" Transformer (4 blocks). Checkpoint is 4.66 GB bf16. No combined total is published.
systems.architecture: MossTTSRealtime — a Qwen3-1.7B-initialised backbone (28 layers, hidden 2048) exposes hidden states to a 4-layer 200 M local Transformer that autoregressively emits RVQ audio tokens. Hierarchical input, text and speech tokens at different levels. Purely autoregressive, no diffusion.
systems.codec: MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer (Causal Audio Tokenizer) — 12.5 Hz frame rate, 16 RVQ codebooks, 24 kHz out
systems.streaming: Yes — streaming text in and audio out; streaming_mossttsrealtime.py ships in the repo. Granularity floor is the 12.5 Hz codec frame (80 ms); the emitted chunk size is not published.
systems.max_generation: 32K context, about 40 minutes of dialogue (max_position_embeddings 40960)
systems.fine_tuning: Yes — official fine-tuning tutorial added 2026-03-26
systems.self_host: Yes — HF and ModelScope, via Transformers 5.0.0; supported in vLLM-Omni since 2026-06-02
systems.benchmarks: Vendor's own table. Seed-TTS-eval: EN WER 1.971% / SIM 68.9%, ZH CER 1.07% / SIM 76.7% (against Qwen3-TTS 1.7B at EN WER 1.5 / SIM 71.45 in the same table). Latency: TTFB 180 ms after warm-up and RTF 0.51 on a single NVIDIA L20 with SDPA + torch.compile.
systems.adoption: 27,999 HF downloads in the trailing 30 days (HF exposes no cumulative figure) and 99 likes, checked 2026-08-01
systems.released: HF repo created 2026-02-09, a day before the MOSS-TTS Family launch. No changelog entry announces it by name; the first naming it is the fine-tuning tutorial on 2026-03-26.

systems.name: dots.tts
systems.cloning: Continuation cloning from reference audio plus transcript
systems.emotion: Implicit from the reference only
systems.runs_on: GPU; VRAM not published
systems.latency_note: Not published
systems.best_for: Speaker similarity as the top priority — the highest average across 24 languages of any open model, with no codec bottleneck at 48 kHz.
systems.watch: Very low adoption, so few community integrations and little third-party validation. Low-resource languages show notably higher error rates.
systems.standout: Highest average speaker similarity across 24 languages of any open model
systems.params: 2 B (Qwen2.5-1.5B AR backbone + AR flow-matching acoustic head)
systems.architecture: Fully continuous end-to-end AR — semantic encoder → LLM → autoregressive flow-matching acoustic head over a 48 kHz AudioVAE. Processes BPE text directly with no phonemization. Three 2 B variants: -base (pretrained), -soar (self-corrective-aligned, default), -mf (MeanFlow-distilled for 2-4 step low latency).
systems.codec: None — no discrete codec tokens anywhere; 48 kHz AudioVAE, mono output
systems.streaming: Claimed as live streaming by the third-party DotsTTS-Studio wrapper; not documented on the official model card
systems.fine_tuning: dots.tts-base is published specifically as the pretrained checkpoint for fine-tuning
systems.self_host: Genuine self-hosted deployment; Apache-2.0. vLLM-Omni integration in progress.
systems.lexicon: No phonemizer — consumes BPE text directly
systems.benchmarks: Seed-TTS-eval: 0.94% Chinese CER with 81.0% speaker similarity; highest average speaker similarity (83.9) across 24 languages among open models per the model card. Recommended 10-32 flow-matching sampling steps; the -mf variant runs at NFE=4. No absolute latency/RTF with hardware published.
systems.adoption: ~1.6 k HF downloads/mo — very low adoption and third-party validation
systems.released: June 2026 (2026-06-03 per community tracker)

systems.name: Chatterbox
systems.variants: Multilingual V3 / Flash, plus a 6-model Single Language Pack
systems.cloning: Zero-shot from ~5 s
systems.emotion: Continuous exaggeration parameter plus CFG weight on the 0.5 B models. The native inline paralinguistic tags belong to the Turbo and Nano rows.
systems.languages_note: 23+ (Multilingual V3) · 1 (the original English 500 M). Turbo and Nano are English-only and have their own rows.
systems.runs_on: CUDA, CPU or Apple MPS — the README loads ChatterboxTTS and ChatterboxMultilingualTTS with device="cuda" | "cpu" | "mps". No CPU throughput figure is published for the 0.5 B models.
systems.latency_note: 75 ms and 6× realtime claimed for Turbo, with no GPU named
systems.best_for: The only major open model shipping neural watermarking by default — the single best answer to the EU AI Act marking duty if you self-host.
systems.watch: The watermark is a property of the official repository, not the weights; an MIT fork can strip the call in one line, and forks that do exist.
systems.standout: The only major open model shipping neural watermarking by default
systems.params: 0.5 B (Multilingual V3, and the original English model). Turbo (350 M) and Nano (110 M) have their own rows. The Single Language Pack is six dedicated 500 M finetunes — zh-cmn, es-mx-latam, pt-br, es-es, pt-pt, hi.
systems.architecture: AR LM on a Llama 3 backbone predicting speech tokens + S3Gen/flow decoder to mel, 10 diffusion steps; trained on ~0.5 M hours of cleaned data. The single-step distilled decoder is the Turbo and Nano rows, not this one.
systems.codec: Not named in the corpus — speech tokens decoded by an S3Gen/flow decoder to mel; 24 kHz output
systems.vram: Not published by Resemble. Corpus deployment matrix lists 8-16 GB inference for the 0.5 B, ~4.5 GB for Turbo, and ~18 GB for LoRA training.
systems.streaming: Not documented as native in the repo README; Resemble's hosted product streams and a community fork (davidbrowne17/chatterbox-streaming) adds streaming
systems.max_generation: ~40 s per chunk before degradation; a separate corpus note gives a max of ~40 s per generation
systems.quantisation: ONNX export published for Turbo (ResembleAI/chatterbox-turbo-ONNX); no ONNX for the multilingual model
systems.fine_tuning: LoRA via a community fork (davidbrowne17/chatterbox-streaming, lora.py) — drop WAVs in a folder and run lora.py; ~10 min of audio, ~1-3 h training, ~18 GB VRAM. Emotion survives fine-tuning per corpus testing.
systems.self_host: Genuine self-hosted deployment; MIT code and weights. pip install chatterbox-tts.
systems.benchmarks: Vendor-run blind test: 65.3% listener preference over ElevenLabs vs 24.5% the other way (Resemble, not independent). Turbo's 75 ms latency and 6x-realtime claims state no GPU, so they are not reproducible. Third-party arena Elo ~1011 cited by blog roundups — unverified.
systems.adoption: 25.8k GitHub stars, 3.4k forks
systems.released: Chatterbox originally May 2025; Multilingual V3 is the current multilingual flagship as of Jul 2026. Only tagged GitHub release is v0.1.2 (2026-06-13); exact V3, Turbo and Nano weight-drop dates not verified (a 2025-12-15 press item announces Turbo).

systems.name: Chatterbox Nano
systems.licence: MIT — code and weights. HF card metadata license: mit; repo LICENSE is MIT (Copyright (c) 2025 Resemble AI). No split code/weights licence.
systems.cloning: Zero-shot from a reference clip, no fine-tuning. Vendor sources disagree on length: the README example passes a 10 s clip and the product page says "10 seconds or more of reference audio", while the Nano/Flash launch post says a 5-second clip.
systems.emotion: Native inline paralinguistic tags — [cough], [laugh], [chuckle] — inherited from Turbo, whose training set Nano shares. The exaggeration / CFG-weight controls of the 0.5 B models are not documented for Nano.
systems.languages_note: English only. HF metadata language: [en]; Model Zoo row reads "English". The 23-language coverage belongs to Chatterbox Multilingual V3, not to this checkpoint.
systems.runs_on: CPU or GPU. Vendor claims 3x realtime on 8 CPU cores (8 threads) and 10x realtime on GPU — no CPU model and no GPU model named for either figure. Loaded as ChatterboxTurboTTS.from_pretrained(device="cpu" | "cuda", nano=True).
systems.latency_note: No time-to-first-audio figure published. Only throughput multiples — 3x realtime on 8 CPU threads, 10x realtime on GPU — neither with hardware named, so neither is reproducible.
systems.best_for: On-device, mobile and air-gapped English TTS where the memory and latency budget rules out a GPU. Resemble's own Model Zoo files it under "On-device / CPU inference, tight latency & memory budgets", and it is the only Chatterbox checkpoint with a published CPU throughput figure.
systems.watch: The 110 M headline is the backbone only — the actual load is ~1.9 GB across three files, which is the number that decides whether it fits your device. Neither speed claim names hardware, so neither is reproducible. English only: if you need any other language you want Multilingual V3, which is a different checkpoint at 5x the size. Every output is PerTh-watermarked by default.
systems.standout: Chatterbox's paralinguistic tags and zero-shot cloning at CPU speed — the family's only edge-targeted checkpoint
systems.params: 110 M as published by Resemble (GitHub README, HF card and product page) — a backbone-only figure. Measured from the shipped safetensors header, t3_nano_v1.safetensors carries 217.5 M F32 parameters: 85.0 M in 12 transformer blocks at 768 hidden, the balance in embedding/output tables including three 50,276 x 768 matrices. With the decoder and voice encoder loaded the pipeline is ~483 M.
systems.architecture: Turbo's architecture in a smaller package: autoregressive speech-token LM over a 12-layer, 768-hidden decoder with learned positional embeddings (8,196 positions) and a 6,563-token speech vocabulary, feeding a distilled S3Gen/flow decoder that produces mel in one step instead of the 10 diffusion steps of the 0.5 B models. Trained on the same dataset as Chatterbox Turbo.
systems.vram: Not published — the product page says only "minimal VRAM". Measured from the published files: t3_nano_v1.safetensors 870 MB + s3gen.safetensors 1.06 GB + ve.safetensors 5.7 MB, so ~1.9 GB of weights must load. The repo also ships an alternative s3gen_meanflow.safetensors (1.06 GB), making a full clone ~3.0 GB.
systems.streaming: Not documented for Nano.
systems.quantisation: None published by Resemble for Nano. The ONNX export ResembleAI/chatterbox-turbo-ONNX is Turbo's, not Nano's.
systems.watermark: PerTh (Perceptual Threshold) neural watermark on every generated file, same as the rest of the Chatterbox line. As with the parent, the watermark call lives in MIT-licensed repository code rather than in the weights, so a fork can remove it.
systems.self_host: Yes — MIT code and MIT weights. pip install chatterbox-tts, then ChatterboxTurboTTS.from_pretrained(device="cpu", nano=True).
systems.benchmarks: None. No MOS, WER, CER or speaker-similarity figures are published for Nano — the vendor evaluation image on the README is Turbo's. The only numbers are vendor throughput multiples with hardware unnamed.
systems.adoption: 18 Hugging Face likes; Hugging Face reports no download count for this repo. The 25.8k stars / 3.4k forks are the shared resemble-ai/chatterbox repository, not Nano.
systems.released: Weights uploaded to Hugging Face 2026-04-14 (repo initial commit, ollieollie); publicly announced alongside Flash in Resemble's "Chatterbox Nano and Flash: Speed at the edge, throughput at scale" post dated 2026-07-06, with the model card refreshed the same day. Card last updated 2026-07-21.

systems.name: Chatterbox Turbo
systems.cloning: Zero-shot from a reference clip
systems.emotion: Native paralinguistic tags inline in the text — cough, laugh, chuckle
systems.languages_note: English only. The 23-language coverage belongs to Chatterbox Multilingual V3.
systems.runs_on: GPU, materially less than Multilingual V3 at 350 M
systems.best_for: Low-latency English voice agents where the 10-step diffusion decoder of the multilingual model is the bottleneck. The distilled single-step decoder is the reason to pick it; if you need any language other than English, this is the wrong row.

systems.self_host: Yes — MIT weights

systems.name: Fish Audio S2 Pro
systems.cloning: Zero-shot; reference requirements undocumented
systems.emotion: 15,000+ free-form inline natural-language tags — the most controllable open TTS shipped
systems.runs_on: GPU, ~10 GB class
systems.latency_note: RTF 0.195 and ~100 ms TTFA on an H200 — one of the few models publishing hardware
systems.best_for: Research and evaluation. Best Seed-TTS-eval error rates of any open model, at 0.54% Chinese CER and 0.99% English WER.
systems.watch: Fish Audio Research License (the HF licence tag is literally "other"). Non-commercial and research use only; commercial use requires a separate licence from business@fish.audio. Routinely reported as MIT — it is not, and Fish's own blog says "open weights, not open source by the OSI definition".
systems.standout: 15,000+ free-form natural-language tags — the most controllable open TTS shipped
systems.params: ~4.6 B total (safetensors 4,561,852,416) — 4 B 'Slow AR' + 400 M 'Fast AR'
systems.architecture: Dual-autoregressive decoder-only transformer over an RVQ neural codec, RL-aligned via GRPO. Native multi-speaker / multi-turn generation.
systems.codec: RVQ (Fish) — 10 codebooks at ~21 Hz frame rate; the dual-AR head handles the depth axis
systems.vram: ~10 GB weights class; benchmarked on a single NVIDIA H200. Corpus deployment matrix lists 17-20 GB FP8 inference and 24-32 GB for training.
systems.streaming: Yes — production streaming via SGLang-Omni
systems.max_generation: No hard limit (corpus deployment matrix)
systems.quantisation: FP8 inference referenced in the corpus deployment matrix; no official quantised build documented

Corpus warns LoRA is NOT recommended on the RL-trained Pro model because it degrades emotion — fine-tune the base model instead, and convert the LoRA to regular weights before inference.
systems.self_host: Self-hostable, but the Fish Audio Research License makes commercial self-hosting require a separate paid licence (business@fish.audio)
systems.multi_speaker: Native multi-speaker / multi-turn generation

RTF 0.195 streaming, ~100 ms time-to-first-audio, 3,000+ acoustic tokens/sec on a single H200 — one of only four open models publishing latency with the hardware named.
systems.adoption: ~295 k HF downloads/mo; 31.8k GitHub stars, 2.7k forks, 732 commits
systems.released: Technical report arXiv 2603.08823, 2026-03-11; HF model card dated ~10-11 March 2026

systems.emotion: 21 discrete emotion tokens, insertable mid-utterance
systems.runs_on: GPU; VRAM not published
systems.latency_note: RTF 0.262 on an H100
systems.best_for: The broadest language coverage of any open model, with genuine inline emotion control.

systems.codec: Multi-codebook — 8 codebooks of 1026 vocab with delay-pattern staggering; the codec is not separately named
systems.streaming: Chunk — Server-Sent Events delivering base64 WAV chunks, sub-second TTFA

systems.name: Kimi-Audio 7B
systems.licence: MIT metadata tag on both checkpoints — but no LICENSE file exists in either HF repo or on GitHub, and the README's licence section covers CODE only (Apache-2.0 for Qwen2.5-derived code, MIT for the rest). No document explicitly grants a licence on the weights.
systems.price_note: Free / self-host. No first-party hosted audio API is documented.
systems.cloning: None exposed. The released generate() API has no speaker, voice-prompt or reference-audio parameter — the model replies in its own trained voice. The paper's 3-second zero-shot cloning belongs to Kimi-TTS, an in-house system used to synthesise training data, which does not ship.
systems.emotion: Prompt-driven only, and only inside a spoken conversation. There is no emotion parameter.
systems.languages_note: Two — English and Mandarin Chinese. No other language is claimed.
systems.runs_on: Single NVIDIA GPU only. The inference API hardcodes torch.cuda.current_device() and loads in bf16 — no CPU, MPS or quantised path exists in the reference implementation. ~9.77 B at bf16 is roughly 20 GB of LLM weights before activations, with a Whisper-large-v3 encoder, a flow-matching detokenizer and a BigVGAN vocoder loading alongside.
systems.best_for: Self-hosted products and research needing one model to LISTEN in English or Mandarin — ASR, audio question answering, captioning, speech emotion recognition, sound-event classification — and optionally reply out loud in the same turn. It is in this matrix to correct a mis-route, not because it is a synthesiser.
systems.watch: IT IS NOT A TTS ENGINE, and Hugging Face says otherwise: both repos carry pipeline_tag text-to-speech, which routes text-to-speech shoppers straight to it. Every documented example takes an AUDIO input; there is no text-in/speech-out quick start, no TTS mode, no voice or speaker control, and two open issues asking for a real TTS path sit unanswered. The weights licence is also undocumented — an MIT tag with no LICENSE file and a README that scopes itself to code. Key the row to the Instruct checkpoint: the base repo is ~3% of downloads and its own card says it "cannot be used directly".
systems.standout: Listens far better than it speaks — an ASR-first model that HF mis-tags as text-to-speech.
systems.params: 9.77 B (9,766,336,640 safetensors total, identical for base and Instruct; HF rounds to 10B). LLM core initialised from Qwen2.5-7B.
systems.architecture: Audio foundation model — hybrid audio input (continuous Whisper-encoder features plus discrete semantic tokens) into a Qwen2.5-7B-initialised transformer with shared multimodal layers and PARALLEL heads emitting text and audio tokens, then a flow-matching detokenizer and BigVGAN vocoder. Pre-trained on 13M+ hours of speech, music and sound.
systems.codec: 12.5 Hz single-codebook VQ on a Whisper-encoder backbone; continuous acoustic features downsampled 50 Hz to 12.5 Hz by an adaptor. Detokenizer is flow matching to mel, then BigVGAN, 24 kHz.
systems.streaming: Chunk-wise flow-matching detokenizer — 1-second autoregressive chunks with a 4-token look-ahead at boundaries. No end-to-end latency, TTFB or RTF figure is published anywhere.
systems.max_generation: In audio mode the code sets max_new_tokens to int(12.5 * 120) minus prompt length unconditionally, overriding the caller — a 120-second budget shared between prompt AND reply, so a long audio question directly shortens the spoken answer.
systems.fine_tuning: Yes — official lightweight finetune_codes for the base checkpoint, released 2025-05-29
systems.self_host: Self-host only
systems.benchmarks: All vendor-reported. ASR WER: LibriSpeech test-clean 1.28, test-other 2.42 (vs Qwen2.5-Omni 2.37 / 4.21); AISHELL-1 0.60 (vs 1.13); Fleurs zh 2.69 / en 4.44. MMAU 61.68 music / 73.27 sound / 60.66 speech. Speech-conversation subjective average 3.90/5, below GPT-4o at 4.06.
systems.adoption: 4,705 GitHub stars, 372 forks. HF — Instruct 395,905 all-time / 97,828 trailing 30 days, 412 likes; base 11,666 all-time / 197 trailing, 95 likes. Roughly 97% of use is the Instruct checkpoint. Figures as of 2026-08-01.
systems.released: 2025-04-25 (inference code, Instruct weights, eval toolkit, technical report); 2025-04-27 (base weights); 2025-05-29 (fine-tuning example)

systems.name: IndexTTS
systems.price_note: Free below the MAU and revenue thresholds
systems.cloning: Zero-shot with speaker identity DISENTANGLED from emotion
systems.emotion: Best-in-class — 8 emotion dimensions controlled three ways (separate reference audio, 0–1 intensity vectors, or free text), plus explicit duration control
systems.runs_on: GPU
systems.latency_note: 2.5 claims a 2.28× improvement over 2, with no absolute figure
systems.best_for: Emotion- and duration-controlled dubbing and localisation, where separating who is speaking from how they feel is the whole job.
systems.watch: Widely reported as Apache-2.0. It is not — the licence carries MAU and revenue thresholds, prohibited-use clauses covering medical, military and biometric surveillance, a bar on improving other commercial AI models, and PRC governing law.
systems.standout: Speaker identity disentangled from emotion, plus 0–1 emotion intensity vectors
systems.architecture: IndexTTS 2: autoregressive with decoupled emotion and speaker-identity features, GPT latent representations, three-stage training, BigVGAN2 decoder, built on the XTTS/Tortoise lineage with a conformer speech-conditioning encoder. IndexTTS 2.5: semantic codec compressed from 50 Hz to 25 Hz, U-DiT replaced by a Zipformer-based semantic-to-mel module, plus RL optimisation.
systems.codec: Semantic codec at 50 Hz in IndexTTS 2, compressed to 25 Hz in 2.5; BigVGAN2 decoder
systems.vram: Not published by Bilibili; the corpus deployment matrix lists ~8-12 GB inference
systems.streaming: Not documented
systems.fine_tuning: Not released for fine-tuning (corpus deployment matrix)
systems.self_host: Self-hostable under the bilibili Model Use License — entities above 100 M MAU or ¥1 B annual revenue must request a separate licence; prohibited-use clauses cover medical, autonomous driving, military, critical infrastructure and large-scale biometric surveillance; cannot be used to improve any other commercial AI model; PRC governing law, Shanghai Arbitration Commission
systems.lexicon: Pinyin annotation supported (IndexTTS 2)
systems.benchmarks: IndexTTS 2.5 claims a 2.28x RTF improvement over IndexTTS 2 at comparable WER and speaker similarity; absolute RTF and hardware not stated.
systems.adoption: 22.3k GitHub stars; ~15.6 k HF downloads/mo
systems.released: IndexTTS2 open-sourced 2025-09-08; IndexTTS 2.5 technical report arXiv 2601.03888, January 2026. IndexTTS 2.5 weight availability under IndexTeam is NOT confirmed.

systems.name: Step-Audio-EditX

systems.latency_note: Not published
systems.best_for: Post-hoc emotion and style editing of existing audio — the only open model doing true iterative editing well.

systems.standout: Iterative re-editing of already-generated audio — 14 emotions, 30+ speaking styles

systems.lexicon: Polyphone pronunciation control

systems.name: VibeVoice
systems.licence: MIT, with usage restrictions layered on in the model card
systems.cloning: Yes, via speaker prompts — the capability that triggered the takedown
systems.emotion: Implicit from context
systems.runs_on: GPU; VRAM not published
systems.latency_note: Not published — the VibeVoice-1.5B model card gives no latency figure
systems.best_for: Long-form multi-speaker generation — 90 minutes with 4 distinct speakers in a single pass, an outlier by more than an order of magnitude.
systems.watch: Microsoft removed the VibeVoice-TTS code on 2025-09-05, two weeks after release, citing use 'inconsistent with the stated intent'. That takedown has since been partially reversed: vibevoice/modular/modeling_vibevoice.py is back on main (its header records that it was copied back from the community fork vibevoice-community/VibeVoice) and docs/vibevoice-tts.md is live. But the 1.5B still shows 'Disabled' under Quick Try in the repo README, no TTS demo script ships in demo/, and VibeVoice-Large weights remain withdrawn (HF 404). Upstream continuity is better than it was, and still not whole.
systems.standout: 90 minutes with four distinct speakers in one pass — an order-of-magnitude outlier
systems.params: VibeVoice-TTS-1.5B: Qwen2.5-1.5B LLM + ~340 M acoustic encoder + ~340 M decoder + ~123 M diffusion head (HF ships 5.41 GB across three bf16 shards, ~2.7 B total tensors) — comparison tables citing both '1.5B' and '3B' are defensible.
systems.architecture: Next-token diffusion over continuous speech tokenizers at a 7.5 Hz frame rate (3,200x downsampling from 24 kHz), with LLM context understanding and CFG at inference
systems.codec: σ-VAE at 7.5 Hz (Microsoft) — continuous rather than discrete tokens, ~3,200x downsampling; this is what enables 90-minute generations
systems.streaming: No — the 1.5B TTS is a batch long-form generator. The streaming model is a separate product (see VibeVoice-Realtime-0.5B).
systems.max_generation: 90 min with up to 4 distinct speakers in a single pass, at 64K context (1.5B) — an outlier by more than an order of magnitude
systems.quantisation: A BitNet-quantised 1.58 GB CPU variant exists for VibeVoice-ASR; no quantised TTS build documented
systems.watermark: Corpus reports an audible AI disclaimer ('This segment was generated by AI') embedded in all output plus an imperceptible watermark. Note the primary open-weights survey lists only the Chatterbox and NeuTTS families as shipping built-in watermarking, so the two sources are not fully consistent.
systems.self_host: Genuine self-hosted deployment, but Microsoft REMOVED the TTS code from the official repo about two weeks after release citing misuse; the weights remain on HF and community forks maintain the code. MIT licence with usage restrictions layered on in the model card.
systems.multi_speaker: Up to 4 distinct speakers in one pass; speaker roles are reported to blend/swap in multi-speaker 1.5 B generations
systems.adoption: 51.7k GitHub stars and 5.7k forks on microsoft/VibeVoice — note that is the whole model family (TTS, ASR, Realtime), not this checkpoint. The 1.5B TTS checkpoint itself draws ~66 k HF downloads/mo.
systems.released: TTS-1.5B 2025-08-25 (ICLR 2026 Oral); VibeVoice-ASR 2026-01-21; VibeVoice-ASR-BitNet 2026-07-23; Azure AI Foundry Labs integration 2026-03-12

systems.name: VibeVoice-Realtime-0.5B
systems.licence: MIT on the checkpoint (HF model card YAML `license: mit`), with an explicit 'this release is not intended or licensed for' list layered on in the model card — the same MIT-plus-restrictions pattern as the 1.5B TTS. Repo LICENSE is also MIT.
systems.cloning: No. Microsoft shipped fixed embedded voice prompts and states it 'Removed acoustic tokenizer to avoid users creating embedding on their own'; voice customisation requires contacting the team. This is the sharpest break from the 1.5B TTS.
systems.emotion: No control surface published — expression is implicit. Timbre and style come from a fixed embedded voice set; 11 distinct English style voices were added 2025-12-16.
systems.languages_note: 1 supported (English). Nine more — German, French, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Dutch, Polish, Portuguese, Spanish — shipped 2025-12-16 but Microsoft labels them exploratory and 'not extensively tested'.
systems.runs_on: GPU or Apple Silicon — Microsoft reports NVIDIA T4 and Mac M4 Pro both reach real-time in its own tests, and warns weaker devices may need further optimisation. No VRAM figure published; the bf16 checkpoint is a single 2.04 GB safetensors file. Docker via NVIDIA PyTorch Container 24.07+ is the documented path.
systems.latency_note: ~300 ms to first audible speech per the HF model card. Microsoft's own repo doc says ~200 ms in its key-features list and ~300 ms for the first speech chunk in the websocket demo note — the two figures are not reconciled. Hardware dependent.
systems.best_for: Agent and live-narration front-ends where speech must start before the text is finished, on hardware as modest as a T4 or an M4 Pro laptop. The streaming counterpart to the 1.5B, not a smaller version of it.
systems.watch: Three catches. (1) No cloning — the acoustic tokenizer was deliberately removed, so you get Microsoft's voices or nothing. (2) 'Streaming text input' is partly aspirational: Microsoft's own TODO in docs/vibevoice-realtime-0.5b.md still has 'Implement streaming text input function to feed new tokens while audio is still being generated' UNCHECKED, so incremental token feeding is not yet a shipped API. (3) The first-audible-latency figure is stated as both ~200 ms and ~300 ms across Microsoft's two pages.
systems.standout: Speech starts in ~300 ms on a T4 or an M4 Pro — but the voice is Microsoft's, not yours
systems.params: 0.5B headline. Qwen2.5-0.5B decoder (hidden 896, 24 layers, 8192 max positions) plus an acoustic tokenizer and a 4-layer diffusion head; the bf16 checkpoint is 2.04 GB, so ~1.0 B total tensors. Same headline-vs-total gap the 1.5B row notes.
systems.architecture: Interleaved, windowed streaming design — incrementally encodes arriving text chunks while continuing diffusion-based acoustic latent generation from prior context. Removes the semantic tokenizer used by the long-form multi-speaker variants and relies solely on the acoustic tokenizer.
systems.codec: Acoustic tokenizer only, 7.5 Hz, 3,200x downsampling from 24 kHz. The semantic tokenizer present in the 1.5B is dropped.
systems.streaming: Yes — streaming text input is the model's reason to exist. Note the incremental token-feed function is still an open TODO upstream.
systems.max_generation: ~10 min, bounded by an 8k-token context (config.json max_position_embeddings = 8192). Single speaker only. Against the 1.5B's 64K / ~90 min, a 9x smaller ceiling.
systems.watermark: Audible AI disclaimer ('This segment was generated by AI') embedded automatically into every synthesized file, plus an imperceptible provenance watermark, per the model card mitigations.
systems.self_host: Genuine. Weights on HF, inference code in microsoft/VibeVoice, plus a Colab notebook and a websocket demo. Unlike the 1.5B TTS, this model's code was never withdrawn.
systems.multi_speaker: No — single speaker only. Microsoft directs multi-speaker users to the long-form variants.
systems.benchmarks: Microsoft's own tables: LibriSpeech test-clean 2.00 WER / 0.695 speaker similarity; SEED test-en 2.05 WER / 0.633. Microsoft notes the model 'is more focused on long-form speech generation' than short-sentence benchmarks.
systems.adoption: 661,602 HF downloads in the trailing 30 days and 1,260 likes — roughly 10x the download volume of the VibeVoice-1.5B TTS checkpoint (66,204).
systems.released: 2025-12-03, per Microsoft's own news entry in the repo README ('2025-12-03: We open-sourced VibeVoice-Realtime-0.5B'). HF repo created 2025-12-04. Experimental multilingual and English style voices added 2025-12-16.

Claims 4x improved real-time throughput vs Zonos-v0.1 with no absolute RTF/TTFA or hardware.
systems.adoption: GitHub repo only ~290 stars — very new and low adoption
systems.released: 2026-06-12 (Zyphra product page)

systems.name: F5-TTS
systems.cloning: Zero-shot, but the reference transcript is required
systems.emotion: None
systems.languages_note: 2 official, with a large community ecosystem

systems.latency_note: RTF ~0.15 on an RTX 4090, commonly cited

systems.streaming: None — not native, chunked inference only

systems.watermark: None — the corpus explicitly names F5-TTS among the open models that ship no watermarking or safety features

systems.name: Orpheus TTS
systems.cloning: Zero-shot
systems.emotion: Inline emotion and intonation tags
systems.languages_note: English primary, plus 7 research language pairs
systems.runs_on: GPU, 3 B class
systems.latency_note: ~200 ms streaming, ~100 ms with input streaming, no hardware stated

Product: Canopy shipped a CLOSED, commercially-hosted Orpheus v1 on GroqCloud on 2026-04-09 with claimed quality improvements and no corresponding open release. The promised 1B, 400M and 150M variants never shipped despite appearing in comparison tables.

systems.params: 3.78 B released (safetensors 3,782,986,752 — a Llama-3.2-3B base plus an expanded audio-token vocabulary, so the "3b" in the repo name understates it). The 1 B / 400 M / 150 M variants remain on the development checklist and have NOT shipped, despite appearing in many comparison tables.
systems.architecture: Llama-3B (Llama 3.2 architecture) backbone predicting SNAC codec tokens, with a CNN-based streaming detokenizer converting SNAC to waveform. Trained on 100k+ hours of English speech.
systems.codec: SNAC — hierarchical multi-scale at 12/24/48 Hz, 7 tokens per frame, 24 kHz output
systems.vram: ~6-8 GB FP16; ~7 GB for Q8_0 GGUF; ~3.5-4 GB for Q4_K_M GGUF; ~12-16 GB for LoRA training with Unsloth; ~24 GB+ for full fine-tuning (corpus deployment notes)

systems.max_generation: Bounded by the context window

systems.fine_tuning: LoRA via Unsloth (1.5x faster, 50% less VRAM, r=64 recommended, 16-bit LoRA not QLoRA 4-bit) or the official HF Trainer/TRL path at sequence length 8192; ~10 min of audio, ~1-2 h training. GGUF export after training. Corpus warns against synthetic training data and reports emotion flattening after LoRA on monotone data.
systems.billing_unit: Per character on Groq hosting — reported at ~$22 / 1M characters (third-party blog, ~Jan 2026, not Groq's own pricing page)
systems.self_host: Genuine self-hosted deployment; Apache-2.0. Also widely available hosted via Groq, Together AI and Baseten.
systems.benchmarks: ~200 ms streaming latency and ~100 ms with input streaming — no hardware stated. Corpus own testing: RTF 0.33 and 2.3 s generation for 7.1 s of audio via llama-server GGUF Q8_0. Blog roundups describe it as best open-source on EmergentTTS-Eval — unverified.
systems.adoption: 6.3k GitHub stars with 118 open issues; Canopy reports over a million downloads and thousands of forks/finetunes
systems.released: March 2025 initial; multilingual research release April 2025; Baseten partnership May 2025. 2026 activity is entirely hosted-side — GroqCloud deployment 2026-01-13 and an April 2026 Saudi Arabic model. No substantive 2026 GitHub releases.

systems.name: NeuTTS Nano

systems.licence: NeuTTS Open License v1.0 (LICENCE file in the checkpoint repo, 'Last Updated: 11 December 2025'). Commercial use is licensed only while you stay under a $5,000,000 annual revenue Threshold; above it, commercial use 'is not licensed under this Agreement' and needs a separate licence from Neuphonic. Covers the weights and the Outputs, not just the code. HF repo tag is license: other on every Nano repo.

Two more traps: the 2,048-token context caps generation at about 30 seconds INCLUDING the reference prompt, and 'multilingual' means four separate models to ship and test, not one.

systems.name: Moshi
systems.cloning: None — fixed voices

systems.codec: Mimi — 24 kHz audio to a 12.5 Hz token rate at 1.1 kbps, fully streaming with 80 ms frames, split semantic/acoustic streams with WavLM semantic distillation

systems.concurrency: Python server: 1 session per instance (asyncio.Lock). Rust backend: 64 simultaneous connections at 3× realtime factor on an L40S.

systems.best_for: Hard-constrained embedded systems with no ML runtime, deterministic memory budgets and genuinely permissive licensing.
systems.watch: In maintenance mode, and audibly dated.
systems.standout: Under 1 MB runtime RAM, BSD-licensed, no ML runtime at all.
systems.params: N/A — non-neural.
systems.architecture: Diphone concatenation (8 kHz cmu_us_kal by default) plus CLUSTERGEN statistical parametric voices; C implementation. An alternative run-time engine for voices developed in the FestVox framework - explicitly not a replacement for Festival, which remains a separate, far larger system.
systems.codec: None — non-neural diphone concatenation.
systems.vram: CPU only. Documented run-time memory under ~1 MB on 32-bit architectures for standard diphone voices (roughly under 2x the size of the generated waveform); 60K core code and a 600K lexicon, against Festival's 2.6M core, 5M lexicon and 16-20M runtime.
systems.streaming: Incremental waveform generation (granularity not specified beyond 'incremental').
systems.quantisation: N/A — non-neural.
systems.fine_tuning: No fine-tuning path; FestVox provides a full voice-building toolchain from recorded data.
systems.self_host: Free open-source local library (CMU permissive, BSD-style). No hosted service exists.
systems.lexicon: Pruned cmulex lexicon ships with the US English voice; additional voices and languages via FestVox.
systems.adoption: A speech-dispatcher output module (flite, festival). Ports exist for Arduino (pschatzmann/arduino-flite) and Android (edu.cmu.cs.speech.tts.flite). Historically the reference 'small TTS'. No download or star figures published.
systems.released: Flite 2.2 is the current stable; no 2026 release observed and no release date is published.

systems.name: Festival
systems.licence: X11-type permissive (CSTR, University of Edinburgh, 1996-2020) for the engine and the US English voices (kal, ked). The UK lexicon (OALD) is restricted to non-commercial use and the British and Spanish voices inherit that restriction. lib/festival.el is GPL; hts_engine is Modified BSD.
systems.cloning: None - new voices are built offline from a recorded corpus via the FestVox toolchain, not cloned from a reference clip.
systems.emotion: None - no emotion tag. SABLE markup exposes PITCH, RATE, VOLUME, EMPH and BREAK only.
systems.languages_note: English (British and American), Spanish and Welsh from CSTR; other groups release additional languages.
systems.runs_on: Workstation and server class Unix - Solaris, SunOS, FreeBSD, Linux; Windows via Cygwin. ~16-20 MB runtime memory. Not an embedded target - that is Flite.
systems.best_for: Voice building and speech research on a workstation: the FestVox toolchain, a Scheme-scriptable engine and four synthesis back ends. Choose Flite instead wherever size or speed is the constraint.
systems.watch: Last release 2.4, December 2014. The UK lexicon (OALD) is non-commercial, so the British and Spanish voices cannot ship in a commercial product - only the US voices kal and ked are free of that restriction.
systems.standout: The Scheme-scriptable research toolchain - with a UK lexicon you may not ship commercially.
systems.params: N/A - non-neural.
systems.architecture: C++ system built on the Edinburgh Speech Tools, driven by a Scheme (SIOD) command interpreter. APIs at shell level, through the Scheme interpreter, as a C++ library, and via an Emacs interface. Back ends include diphone concatenation, unit selection (clunits), Clustergen and hts_engine.
systems.codec: None - non-neural concatenative and statistical parametric synthesis.
systems.vram: CPU only. ~16-20 MB runtime memory, 2.6 MB core code and a 5 MB lexicon (figures from Flite's own published Flite-vs-Festival comparison table).
systems.quantisation: N/A - no neural weights.
systems.fine_tuning: No fine-tuning path; FestVox provides a full voice-building toolchain from recorded data.
systems.self_host: Free open-source local system (X11-type licence). No hosted service exists.
systems.ssml: SABLE XML/SGML markup, not SSML. Supported tags: LANGUAGE, SPEAKER, AUDIO, MARKER, BREAK, DIV, PRON, SAYAS, EMPH, PITCH, RATE, VOLUME, ENGINE. The manual notes the SABLE definition is still in development.
systems.lexicon: CMU lexicon for US English; the SABLE PRON tag overrides pronunciation. The UK lexicon is OALD, restricted to non-commercial use.
systems.multi_speaker: SABLE SPEAKER tag switches voice within a single document.
systems.released: 2.4 - December 2014 (CSTR download page). The festvox/festival GitHub mirror carries no tags.

systems.name: ETI-Eloquence
systems.cloning: None
systems.emotion: Pitch and rate
systems.runs_on: Windows, inside screen readers
systems.latency_note: Effectively instantaneous
systems.best_for: Still shipping in JAWS 2026 and still winning on merit at 800 words per minute — the clearest evidence that naturalness is not the objective function in accessibility.
systems.watch: A 1990s formant synthesiser. It sounds like one, and its users do not care.
systems.standout: Still winning at 800 words per minute for screen-reader users.
systems.params: N/A — formant synthesiser, no neural model.

systems.codec: None — formant synthesis.
systems.streaming: Yes — streaming supported; granularity not documented.
systems.quantisation: N/A — no neural weights.

systems.name: VITS / Matcha / Glow-TTS
systems.cloning: None natively
systems.emotion: None
systems.languages_note: Piper covers 30+; the Fairseq VITS collection covers ~1,100
systems.runs_on: CPU-viable at RTF under 0.1; ONNX exports standard; Raspberry Pi class
systems.latency_note: Well under RTF 0.1 on modest CPU
systems.best_for: The actual workhorses of production offline TTS — every Home Assistant install, every accessibility tool, every embedded product. Boring, tiny, permissive and reliable.
systems.watch: No cloning, no emotion, and per-voice models must be trained individually.
systems.standout: RTF under 0.1 on a Raspberry Pi, MIT, ~1,100 languages.
systems.params: 18–90 M per voice (compiled reference figure for the VITS / Matcha / Glow / FastSpeech2 family). Matcha-TTS is separately reported at ~10–40 M elsewhere in the corpus.
systems.architecture: Generation-2: neural acoustic model plus a separate vocoder. VITS specifically is end-to-end — a conditional VAE with adversarial training, a single feed-forward pass from text to waveform. Matcha-TTS decodes with an ODE solver in 2–5 steps. Glow-TTS internals are not stated in the corpus.
systems.codec: None — no neural audio codec. Mel spectrogram plus vocoder, and VITS goes end-to-end text to waveform.
systems.vram: CPU-viable, Raspberry-Pi class; ONNX export is the standard distribution format. No VRAM figure published.
systems.streaming: Chunk/sentence — VITS-style end-to-end is a single feed-forward pass streamed chunked; Piper's VITS generator yields sentence-level chunks. Not documented for Matcha or Glow-TTS.
systems.quantisation: ONNX is the standard export format; the piper1-gpl VITS line added quantized models. No family-level quantisation table is published.
systems.fine_tuning: Per-voice models must be trained individually. Piper ships a VITS training recipe with published checkpoints for transfer learning.
systems.self_host: Free open-source self-host (MIT). No hosted service — deployment is via ONNX Runtime / sherpa-onnx.
systems.multi_speaker: Multi-speaker VITS checkpoints are standard in the sherpa-onnx zoo — VCTK 109 speakers, aishell3 174, Chinese multi-speaker up to 804, and vits-piper-en_US-libritts_r-medium at 904 speakers. This is speaker selection, not dialogue.
systems.benchmarks: Compiled reference states 'well under RTF 0.1 on modest CPU' with no hardware named. Elsewhere in the corpus, feed-forward VITS is cited at RTF 0.015 (67x realtime) 'even on modest GPUs' — GPU not named. The only named-hardware measurement in the corpus is for Piper, a VITS implementation carried as its own row: Picovoice (2026-07-14, AMD Ryzen 7 5700X, 64 GB RAM, ~200 simulated voice-assistant utterances) 0.54x core-hour ratio, 1,510 ms first-token-to-speech, 2.6 GB peak memory, 61 MB model.
systems.adoption: Described in the compiled reference as the actual workhorse of production offline TTS — Home Assistant installs, accessibility tooling and embedded products. The Fairseq VITS collection spans ~1,100 languages. sherpa-onnx carries VITS (including all Piper voices), Matcha and multi-speaker VITS checkpoints across Linux/macOS/Windows/Android/iOS/HarmonyOS/WASM and x86/ARM32/aarch64/RISC-V. No download or star figures published.
systems.released: Generation-2 era, 2018–2023 per the compiled reference. No per-model release dates for VITS, Matcha-TTS or Glow-TTS appear in the corpus.

systems.name: LiveKit Agents
systems.licence: Framework Apache-2.0; turn-detector models under the bespoke LiveKit Model License
systems.price_note: Free to self-host; $0.0100 / agent-session minute on LiveKit Cloud (orchestration only)
systems.cloning: Inherited from the chosen TTS vendor
systems.emotion: Inherited from the chosen TTS or realtime provider
systems.languages_note: Provider-dependent; the bundled turn detector itself covers 14 languages with thresholds auto-applied per detected language
systems.runs_on: Self-host the SFU and agents on Kubernetes or Docker, or LiveKit Cloud
systems.latency_note: Turn detector v1 (audio) returns a prediction within ~1 s, falling back to v1-mini on timeout; the deprecated text detector ran 50–160 ms per turn on typical hardware
systems.best_for: Production voice agents at scale where you want to swap providers freely, own the transport and keep a self-host path. The strongest turn-taking tooling in the segment — adaptive interruption mode distinguishes genuine interruptions from backchannelling, so 'mm-hmm' does not stop the agent, and false-interruption recovery resumes speech once silence confirms no real interruption.
systems.watch: The $0.0100/min agent-session fee is orchestration only and is a small fraction of true all-in cost — you assemble and pay for every component separately. The turn-detector models ship under a bespoke, non-OSI LiveKit Model License, not the framework's Apache-2.0, so verify it before commercial redistribution. Self-hosting the SFU brings WebRTC operational complexity.
systems.standout: Adaptive interruption that tells backchannels from genuine interruptions.
systems.architecture: Provider-agnostic orchestration supporting both cascaded STT→LLM→TTS and native realtime models in one framework. Five turn-detection strategies: the turn-detector model (default, audio plus semantic on top of VAD), VAD-only for minimum latency, STT endpointing, realtime-LLM server-side detection, and manual push-to-talk over RPC. The v1 audio detector encodes user audio directly rather than depending on transcripts; the older text-based detector is deprecated.
systems.streaming: Yes — WebRTC-native bidirectional, which is the correct transport for lossy last-mile networks
systems.billing_unit: Per agent-session minute, orchestration only — STT, LLM and TTS are billed on top. Data transfer $0.12/GB on Build and Ship, $0.10/GB on Scale; US local numbers 1 free then $1.00/month; US local inbound $0.01/min after allotment; third-party SIP $0.004/min falling to $0.003/min.
systems.free_tier: Build $0/month, no credit card: 1,000 agent-session minutes, 5,000 WebRTC minutes, 50 GB transfer and $2.50 of inference credits (~50 min). Ship from $50/month adds 5,000 agent minutes; Scale from $500/month adds 50,000.
systems.self_host: Yes — the SFU and the Agents framework are Apache-2.0 and self-hostable anywhere. Turn-detector v1-mini runs locally on CPU with minimal resources; turn-detector v1 (audio) is served on LiveKit Inference rather than locally.
systems.released: Agents framework on the 1.5.x line as of 2026; LiveKit Cloud is GA

systems.name: Pipecat / Pipecat Cloud
systems.licence: BSD-2-Clause (framework and the Smart Turn v3 model)
systems.price_note: Free to self-host; Pipecat Cloud $0.01–0.03 / active agent-minute ($0.0005–0.0015 reserved)
systems.cloning: Inherited from the chosen TTS vendor
systems.emotion: Inherited from the chosen TTS vendor
systems.languages_note: Provider-dependent; the bundled Smart Turn v3 endpointing model is multilingual
systems.runs_on: Self-host anywhere Python runs, or Pipecat Cloud; Smart Turn v3 runs on CPU
systems.latency_note: Smart Turn v3 endpointing ~12 ms CPU inference, ~65 ms end-to-end on a standard Pipecat Cloud 1x instance via LocalSmartTurnAnalyzerV3
systems.best_for: Teams that want maximum provider optionality under the most permissive licence in the segment, or that want the reserved-instance pricing model for always-warm agents. Free 1:1 WebRTC voice transport is a genuine cost advantage over LiveKit's data-transfer billing.
systems.watch: Pipecat Cloud's per-minute price covers the agent container only — every model call is billed by the underlying vendor, so the headline rate is nowhere near all-in. Python-only. Turn-taking event tooling is less mature than LiveKit's, with no published backchannel-versus-interruption discrimination mode.
systems.standout: BSD-2 including its bundled 8 M turn detector, ~12 ms on CPU.
systems.params: N/A for the framework; the bundled Smart Turn v3 turn-detection model is 8 M parameters, 8 MB int8 ONNX
systems.architecture: Pipeline/frame-based orchestration over cascaded or native-realtime models, with 25+ STT providers, 30+ LLMs and 25+ TTS providers, plus Pipecat Flows for structured stateful dialog. Ships Smart Turn v3, an 8M-parameter Whisper-Tiny encoder with a shallow linear classifier that reads the raw waveform rather than the transcript, so endpointing never waits for STT.
systems.streaming: Yes — transports are Daily (WebRTC), LiveKit (WebRTC), FastAPI WebSocket, WhatsApp and local
systems.billing_unit: Per agent-container minute by profile — agent-1x (0.5 vCPU, 1 GB) $0.01/min active or $0.0005/min reserved; agent-2x (1 vCPU, 2 GB) $0.02 or $0.001; agent-3x (1.5 vCPU, 3 GB) $0.03 or $0.0015. Separate meters: WebRTC voice 1:1 free, WebRTC voice/video $0.004 per participant-minute, SIP $0.003–$0.02/min, PSTN $0.018/min, audio recording $0.005/min, audio+video $0.01349/min, Krisp VIVA noise elimination free for the first 10k min/month then $0.0015/min. 80+ external LLM/STT/TTS providers bill you directly.
systems.concurrency: Unlimited
systems.self_host: Yes — the whole framework is BSD-2-Clause Python and self-hostable; also distributed by NVIDIA via build.nvidia.com as a voice-agent framework
systems.benchmarks: Smart Turn v3 trained on 270k training and 31.5k test samples sourced from Liva AI, Midcentury and MundoAI. Inference ~12 ms on CPU per the Pipecat blog, and ~65 ms end-to-end on a standard Pipecat Cloud 1x instance per the Pipecat Cloud docs — the fastest turn-detection inference in this survey by an order of magnitude. Per-language accuracy is unpublished. The framework markets 'ultra-low latency' with no headline end-to-end figure.
systems.released: Pipecat reached v1.0; Pipecat Cloud reached GA in January 2026. Smart Turn v3 released December 2025.

systems.name: Vapi
systems.price_note: $0.05 / min platform fee — models billed on top
systems.cloning: Inherited from the chosen TTS vendor
systems.emotion: Inherited from the chosen TTS vendor
systems.languages_note: Provider-dependent; no platform language list published
systems.runs_on: Cloud only
systems.latency_note: Average under 500 ms, claimed on Vapi's own homepage with no measurement conditions
systems.best_for: The fastest managed path to production telephony agents with enterprise compliance — SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI, SSO/OAuth/RBAC and data residency — without building orchestration yourself.

Bringing your own provider API keys waives the pass-through entirely, turning Vapi into a pure $0.05/min orchestration layer; that is the cheapest way to use it and is easy to miss. HIPAA at $2,000/month and Zero Data Retention at $1,000/month are steep fixed adders for regulated buyers, and Build retains calls for only 14 days.
systems.standout: Bring your own keys and it becomes a pure $0.05/min orchestrator.
systems.architecture: Cascaded orchestration by default — you pick STT, LLM and TTS — with support for native realtime models, and a large third-party integration surface across telephony, AI providers and business tools
systems.streaming: Yes
systems.billing_unit: Per call minute as a platform fee only. STT, LLM and TTS provider costs are passed through on top, or waived entirely if you bring your own API keys. SMS and chat $0.005 per message. Scale is an annual contract: fixed platform fee plus committed volume at volume-based per-minute rates.
systems.concurrency: 10 concurrent lines included on Build, then $10 per additional line per month
systems.self_host: No — cloud only
systems.data_policy: 14-day call and 30-day chat retention on Build. Zero Data Retention is a $1,000/month add-on and HIPAA compliance a $2,000/month add-on, on either plan.
systems.benchmarks: No comparable published figure. Vapi's homepage claims average latency under 500 ms and 99.9% enterprise uptime; measurement conditions, region and percentile are all unstated.
systems.adoption: Vendor-stated: 1 billion calls handled and 2.5M+ agents launched. Named production users include Amazon Ring (routing 100% of inbound volume), Intuit, ServiceTitan and New York Life.

systems.name: Retell AI
systems.cloning: Inherited from the chosen TTS vendor
systems.emotion: Inherited from the chosen TTS vendor
systems.languages_note: Provider-dependent; no platform language list published

Add-ons: knowledge base +$0.005/min, PII removal +$0.01/min, AI quality assurance $0.10/min with the first 100 minutes free. Chat agents from $0.002 per message. Subscriptions: extra concurrency $8.00 per call per month, verified phone numbers $10.00/month.

systems.self_host: No — cloud only

systems.name: Bland AI
systems.licence: Proprietary SaaS; on-prem and VPC deployment at Enterprise
systems.price_note: $0.11–0.14 / min all-in (LLM, STT and TTS included)
systems.cloning: Not documented
systems.emotion: Not documented
systems.runs_on: Bland's own infrastructure; on-premises or VPC at Enterprise
systems.best_for: Buyers who want one predictable per-minute number with no model pass-throughs, and regulated buyers who need on-prem or VPC deployment — rare among managed voice platforms.
systems.watch: The latency claim has no number, no conditions and no third-party verification. Vertical integration is the trade: you cannot swap in a better LLM or TTS, and no model details, language list or voice-cloning capability are published at all. $0.11–$0.14/min all-in is higher than a tuned LiveKit or Pipecat stack, but it is one number rather than five.
systems.standout: One all-in per-minute rate, no pass-throughs, plus Enterprise on-prem.
systems.architecture: Vertically integrated — Bland runs its own models end to end rather than orchestrating third parties, the opposite strategy to Vapi, Retell and LiveKit
systems.streaming: Yes
systems.billing_unit: Per minute, all-inclusive — the rate covers LLM, STT and TTS with no token charges and no model-provider pass-throughs. Start $0.14/min with no platform fee; Build $0.12/min plus $299/month; Scale $0.11/min plus $499/month; Enterprise custom with dedicated infrastructure, BAA, SSO, data residency and a forward-deployed engineer. BYO telephony (a Twilio account or SIP trunks from any provider) is supported and avoids transfer fees.

systems.benchmarks: No comparable published figure. Bland claims 'the lowest latency on the planet' with no supporting number and no measurement conditions.

systems.name: Phonic
systems.cloning: Not documented

systems.name: Twilio ConversationRelay
systems.price_note: $0.07 / min, on top of Programmable Voice minutes

Pay-as-you-go, no commitments.

systems.benchmarks: Deepgram's own published figures for Flux end-of-turn detection: 260 ms P50, median under 300 ms, p95 1.5 s, with transcript updates every quarter second, and a claimed 200–600 ms reduction in overall agent response latency versus a traditional STT-plus-VAD pipeline. Hardware and region are unstated, but Deepgram is one of only two vendors in the segment publishing both a median and a p95 for a component.
